title: Boundary-Crossing Instruments — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Boundary-Crossing Instruments' rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: in Origin, the repeat-rate dial gathered from Frequency-Time Duality where the page names it, and one made walk up to the wall at infinite ratio, a ratio knob and a slope knob on one compressor, ending in a blind test of which ruler the ear uses. I grow when the Three-Layer Interface earns a piece that tests it rather than labels it. I never hold the entry's words.

offers.what: List the repeat-rate worlds in the order they sit on the axis: 'pitch, slapback, echo, rhythm, and sub-rhythmic pulse' (the text has echo before slapback). The gathered delay proof puts slapback at 80 to 150 ms and distinct echo at 150 to 800 ms, so a reader sweeping its dial meets them in that order.

Say which axes the slope is on: 'the slope of the transfer function in decibels'. Only on decibel axes is the slope one number equal to 1/R. The piece's check measured a 4:1 curve on linear amplitude axes: its slope is 0.149 at 6 dB over the threshold and 0.031 at 24 dB over, against 0.25 everywhere in decibels. The right coordinate system here takes two choices, slope instead of ratio and decibels instead of amplitude, and the second one is unstated.

verdicts.why: Lets the ear check the paragraph's one-dial claim, and could fail if the repeats never became a pitch; the caption honestly warns its zone labels are drawn by code. Note: the caption should also say the sketch's six names are not the page's five, and that sub-rhythmic pulse lies past its 5 s end.

verdicts.why: A real test that walks up, and every number rechecks; two sentences are not honest. (a) The reveal names the slope's ruler from one tie: all five pairs rated 'barely', check failed included, still reads 'Your ear used the slope's ruler'; name a ruler only if the check was 'the same', 1/2 rated above 20/inf, and 20/inf within one step of 10/20, otherwise say the answers pick no ruler. (b) Step 3's 'like most hardware it gets a notch' is unverified and the dbx 160X runs continuously 1:1 to inf:1 to -1:1; drop the clause or name the dbx as hardware that took the slope's road.

pieces.title: One delay, six worlds · Frequency-Time Duality's May sketch
pieces.caption: **One dial, several worlds: the 2024 boundary this page says came first.** Press play and drag the delay from 5 seconds down to half a millisecond. Noise pulses go into one delay line with feedback, and the only thing that changes is how often the repeats come. Somewhere along the way they stop being repeats and become a pitch. This is Frequency-Time Duality's May sketch, gathered as it was. Its zone names are drawn in by the code at fixed edges, so listen before you read the label. For a test that leaves the crossing to your ear, Dissolutions' face has a blind glide from 4 to 64 Hz where you mark where loudness becomes a sound.

pieces.title: One compressor, two knobs · a walk up to the wall at infinite ratio
pieces.caption:
**Is the wall at infinite ratio in the compressor, or in the number?** A drum loop made from noise and sine goes through one compressor whose curve you can set two ways, by ratio and by slope. Six steps: the curve as a plain wire; a threshold and a ratio; a ratio knob's last stretch, where 20:1 to 100:1 takes 78% of a linear knob's travel to move the loudest hit 0.96 dB and ∞ needs a notch; the slope knob, which sets the same curve in equal decibels per turn, 1 to 0; a morph between two settings, which walked in ratio hits ∞:1 the moment it leaves 2:1; and last a blind test of five unnamed pairs, rated by ear and then revealed. 20:1 to ∞:1 is infinitely far apart in ratio and 0.05 in slope, the same as 10:1 to 20:1. On this loop each moves the crest, its peak over its average, by about half a decibel (0.55 and 0.54 dB at 48 kHz). Loudness is matched in the test.

out = T + s × (in − T),  s = 1 ÷ R

(level out, dB) = (threshold) + (slope) × ((level in) − (threshold)), with (slope) = 1 ÷ (ratio)
